text:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, maid and cook, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Good morning, Mademoiselle Häfeli. Please sit down. I am sorry to keep you up. Monsieur Monnier was found dead in his atelier this night, and I must ask everyone in the house the same questions. You are the maid and the cook here?

ROSA: Ja, Herr Inspektor. Maid and cook. I came up from the Emmental as a young woman. I keep the kitchen and the ground floor and the linen. Madame says I am the only one who does not leave the silver dirty.

MATTHEY: Tell me about Monsieur Monnier, as a master.

ROSA: He was strict, with his watches and with everybody. He would not have a thing out of place on his bench, and he did not like a noise in the house while he was working. But he was good to me when my mother was ill, and he never mentioned it.

MATTHEY: Tell me about your clock.

ROSA: It is the American clock on the shelf over the stove. It is cheap, and it is loud. I keep it fast on purpose. When the temple struck ten, my kitchen clock showed a quarter past ten. So that nothing in this house is ever late. The soup is never late, the coffee is never late, Madame is never kept waiting.

MATTHEY: Did anyone come down to the kitchen during the evening?

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at twenty-three minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She is a quiet girl. She keeps her feelings out of her face, the same as her work.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything from the rest of the house?

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at twelve minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and stop at one minute past eleven by my kitchen clock. It was Chopin. Madame plays Chopin when she is troubled, and I think she was troubled.

MATTHEY: And the hall clock?

ROSA: I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed three minutes past eleven. The old clock in the hall has its own face and its own ways, and I do not touch it.

MATTHEY: Tell me what happened when you went up to the atelier.

ROSA: Madame said the master must come down for the toast, so I went up to fetch him. I opened the door, and I saw him on the floor by his bench. Herrgott. I did not touch him.

MATTHEY: You seem frightened, Mademoiselle.

ROSA: I am frightened of the police, Herr Inspektor, I will say so. I have never sat in a room with a police officer. But Madame has been good to me, and I will not say anything against her. She has borne a great deal, and she is a good woman.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you wish to add?

ROSA: Only that I have told you the truth about the clock. Everyone in this house knows I keep it fast. Nothing in my kitchen was late tonight, Herr Inspektor. Nothing was late.
